The selected routes, copy, synchronized in-process state, injectable clock, digest storage, CSRF defense, and session-generation interface are proposed implementation decisions, not additional requirements or evidence of an implemented application.

For accepted requests for an existing synthetic account, a reset link is recorded privately in the in-memory notification sink; no public response reports whether a link was issued. Unknown accounts are never created from a reset request.

Until sign-in authentication and session creation are specified, multiple synthetic active sessions can be registered by test fixtures; every earlier session must be rejected after a successful reset. This does not claim that sign-in success is implemented.

The one-process store and sink are volatile exercise mechanisms; no durable persistence, real mail delivery, production account integration, cross-worker consistency, deployment, or deployment workflow is implied. architecture_summary: Proposed Python 3.12 Flask application factory composes Jinja server-rendered routes/templates, a recovery service, an injected timezone-aware UTC clock, synchronized in-process synthetic account/request/token/session state, and a private in-memory notification sink. GET /sign-in renders the image-observed sign-in surface and links to GET /password/forgot; no sign-in success behavior is specified. GET /password/forgot renders a labeled request form; POST /password/forgot accepts an email and CSRF proof, normalizes it for private lookup, and returns the same public status, content, and navigation for otherwise equivalent valid existing, unknown, and at-limit submissions. Under one lock, an eligible existing account can record no more than five accepted requests in the rolling preceding hour, with timestamps strictly newer than now minus one hour; an accepted request issues a cryptographically random opaque link to the owner's private sink entry, storing only a token digest and exact UTC issuance time. GET /password/reset/<token> checks but never consumes the link and renders a proposed labeled new-password form or a non-success state. POST /password/reset/<token> validates input and CSRF, rechecks digest, unused status, and now < issued_at + 30 minutes (ineligible at the exact boundary); under the shared lock a successful completion updates only the token's account password hash, consumes the token, advances that account's session generation so all earlier active server-side sessions fail on next access, and records one owner-directed success notification before returning a server-rendered success state. Concurrent replay cannot succeed twice. Internal records are synthetic Account(account_id, normalized_email, password_hash, session_generation), ResetRequest(account_id, accepted_at), ResetToken(digest, account_id, issued_at, used), Session(server_side_id, account_id, saved_generation), and Notification(kind, recipient, timestamp, link only for reset_link); no account inventory, token inspection, or sink endpoint is public. Proposed controls include CSRF on POST, secure secret/cookie configuration, escaped templates, a trusted reset-link origin, suppression of tokens, emails, passwords, and link URLs in logs or public output, and local privacy-safe counters. The shared lock protects in-process check-and-write operations but is neither durable nor multi-worker safe; restart discards all state, so there is no exercise migration. Production substitution would separately need durable transactional stores/outbox, external account and message integrations, migration, retention, key management, distributed coordination, abuse defenses, delivery assurance, and monitoring; none is authorized here. Python/Flask/Jinja is preferred over a client-only SPA to meet server-rendering requirements; a single injected in-memory store and sink is preferred over external database/mail for the bounded exercise; random digested tokens over sequential/plaintext tokens, rolling per-account timestamps over fixed-hour buckets, and a server-side session generation over clearing one browser cookie enforce the approved recovery rules. Pytest is a future implementation gate, not a claimed result. No deployment target or workflow is proposed.

tasks.title: Build Flask sign-in shell and recovery entry
tasks.description: Set up a Python 3.12 Flask application factory and server-rendered templates. Render the observed sign-in panel and a working Forgot password? link to a server-rendered reset-request form. Keep sign-in authentication and successful-login destination unspecified; the wireframe does not define them. Proposed recovery-page copy and styling are not wireframe facts.
acceptance_criteria: On Python 3.12, Flask serves rendered HTML for the sign-in and reset-request pages; a browser can follow the sign-in Forgot password? link to the request form.

The sign-in page displays a centered bordered panel with bold Sign in heading, labeled Email address and Password fields with name@example.com and masked ******** placeholders, a blue underlined Forgot password? link below the password field, a wide dark Sign in button below the link, and a muted No account? Contact your administrator. footer; exact pixels and color values are not asserted.

tasks.title: Implement injectable synthetic recovery state
tasks.description: Provide in-process synthetic accounts with hashed passwords, synchronized request timestamps and token-digest records, an injected UTC clock, a test-inspectable but nonpublic notification sink, and server-side account/session-generation checks. Allow fixtures to register multiple sessions without inventing sign-in success behavior. Keep sensitive state out of visitor responses.
acceptance_criteria: A test can construct a synthetic account with a hashed password, register two independent active sessions, record and inspect internal reset-link and reset-success notification kinds, and observe no production account or external notification dependency.
A session check rejects a registered session whose saved generation differs from its account's current generation; no public endpoint exposes the account inventory, token state, or notification sink.

tasks.title: Implement private reset-request eligibility and link issuance
tasks.description: Connect the server-rendered request form to a service using the synthetic state. Normalize an email for lookup, count accepted requests per existing account over the preceding rolling hour under a shared lock, and privately issue an opaque single-account link into the in-memory sink only for an accepted existing-account request. Present an account-independent generic response for equivalent valid existing, unknown, and at-limit requests; never expose issuance or throttle decisions.
acceptance_criteria: Equivalent valid requests for an existing account, an unknown account, and an existing account at its cap have identical public status, rendered content, and response/navigation class, without account or throttle disclosure.

With controlled time, the first five requests for an existing account in a rolling hour each record one reset link; a sixth inside that hour records none and receives the same generic response; once the oldest accepted request is outside the preceding hour, another can issue a link.

tasks.title: Complete single-use resets and post-reset effects
tasks.description: Implement server-rendered new-password, ineligible-link, and success states. Check opaque token eligibility against its private digest and exact issue time, then recheck on POST and atomically update the token's account password hash, consume the token, advance that account's session generation, and append an owner-directed success notice before reporting success. Reject expired, malformed, and replayed tokens without successful side effects. A GET never consumes a token; do not assume a specified login destination or password-complexity rule.
acceptance_criteria: An eligible unused link submitted before issue_time + 30 minutes updates only its associated account's password and succeeds once; at exactly issue_time + 30 minutes or later it is ineligible, and a consumed link cannot complete a second reset.

For an account with multiple previously active sessions, each successful reset makes every earlier session fail subsequent authorization checks and records one owner-directed reset-success notice in the private sink for that success; rejected or replayed submissions neither change a password nor record a success notice.

Two submissions of one eligible link cannot both succeed, and rendered success is returned only after the password change, token consumption, session invalidation, and notification entry complete in-process.

tasks.title: Verify sign-in and recovery behavior with pytest
tasks.description: Add pytest coverage using the Flask client, synthetic accounts, controlled issue-time clock, multiple session fixtures, and private sink inspection. Verify the sign-in visual hierarchy and navigation, generic response equality including at the cap, rolling-hour issuance, token use/replay and exact expiry boundary, password change, all-session invalidation, and notification after each success. Treat risk items as prospective checks, not recorded defects.
acceptance_criteria: Running pytest checks the rendered sign-in evidence and recovery navigation, existing/unknown/at-limit public response equality, first-five/sixth-request/rolling-hour link counts, and absence of public notification-sink disclosure.

Running pytest checks token submission just before, at, and after issue_time + 30 minutes; replay and competing submissions; correct password update; invalidation of multiple earlier active sessions; and one owner notice for each successful reset without a notice for rejected attempts.

tasks.title: Document production limitations and verify no deployment
tasks.description: Document synthetic accounts, volatile single-process account/token/request/session state, in-memory rather than externally delivered notifications, restart and cross-worker limitations, and unresolved production hardening. Review delivered actions and changed paths to verify no application deployment and no added deployment workflow. This is documentation and negative-scope verification, not deployment authorization.
acceptance_criteria: Project documentation explicitly identifies synthetic-account and in-memory-notification limitations, lost state at restart, lack of cross-worker durability, and the absence of a production account or mail integration; it does not claim production readiness.
Review of delivery actions finds no performed deployment, and review of repository changes finds no added deployment workflow.
